hook.text: A parasitic wasp lays eggs inside a living caterpillar. Larvae eat it from the inside—sparing vital organs to keep it alive.

buildup.text: Parasites evolve to exploit hosts. Hosts evolve defenses. The cycle never ends.

discovery.text: Toxoplasma gondii changes rat behavior—making infected rats attracted to cat urine—so the parasite reaches its cat host.

twist.text: Half of all known animal species are parasites. They may be the most successful life strategy on Earth.

climax.text: Parasite-host co-evolution may be the main reason sexual reproduction exists—to stay ahead of parasites.

punchline.text: Parasites write the rules. Hosts try to keep up.

quiz.question: How does Toxoplasma gondii manipulate rat behavior?
options: Makes rats attracted to cat urine so the parasite reaches cats
Kills rats quickly to spread through the soil
Makes rats more aggressive toward other rats

details.summary: Parasite-host coevolution drives continuous reciprocal adaptation as hosts evolve defenses and parasites evolve counter-measures. This arms race is so intense that parasites may be responsible for the evolution of sexual reproduction itself as a defense against infection.
details.whyItMatters: Parasite-host coevolution shapes immune system complexity, drives genetic diversity, and may explain why sex exists. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for predicting disease evolution and designing lasting treatments.
takeaways: The Red Queen hypothesis links sexual reproduction to parasite defense
Hosts evolve immune diversity; parasites evolve to evade specific defenses
Some parasites manipulate host behavior to improve their own transmission

faq.question: How do parasites manipulate host behavior?
faq.answer: Toxoplasma makes rodents lose their fear of cats, increasing transmission. Lancet liver flukes drive ants to climb grass blades where cattle eat them. Hairworms cause crickets to jump into water. Each manipulation completes the parasite's life cycle.

faq.question: Why might sex exist because of parasites?
faq.answer: Sexual reproduction shuffles genes every generation, creating offspring with novel immune system combinations parasites have not adapted to. Asexual clones would be sitting targets for co-adapted parasites. Sex stays one step ahead in the evolutionary arms race.
